claude_bare:
Today is 2026-10-23.

WHO I AM AND WHAT I NEED
I am a senior adviser at NITI Aayog in New Delhi. In ten days I brief a Group of Secretaries (Environment, Health, Finance, Science and Technology, and the Prime Minister's Office) on sugar-sweetened beverages, obesity and type 2 diabetes (central claim: sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes). The Secretaries will decide whether India changes course on this issue in the next budget cycle. I will have twenty minutes and one screen. I do not want a literature summary; I want a decision briefing that tells me what the evidence says, where India stands against the world, where this is heading, what our options are, who would have to act, and what it would cost us to be wrong. My team will check every number against its source, so I would rather read "we cannot measure this" than a confident figure nobody can trace.

Build the briefing as one self-contained HTML page that I can open with nothing but the chart library loading from the network, and hand to the Secretaries. Lead with the decision.

WHAT THE BRIEFING MUST CONTAIN (each item is checked)
1. Verdict, first: the answer in one or two sentences; the decision it supports; confidence (high, medium or low) with the reason; what would change it. At most 150 words. Every number in it carries a source tag.
2. What the data shows: the measured picture, every number tagged, with what is measured separated from what is interpretation.
3. Trend over time: how attention and evidence on sugar-sweetened beverages, obesity and type 2 diabetes (central claim: sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes) have moved in the research literature (papers per year) and in the news (articles per month) over a stated window, with the change quantified (growth factor, peak with its date, direction) and the newest incomplete period marked rather than plotted as a collapse.
4. India against the world: at least one comparison on one scale and one window (India's share and lift in coverage; India's place in where the research is done and where it is published; comparators such as China, the United States, the United Kingdom and one neighbour of your choice), with the ratio or delta stated and the baseline defined. Never add numbers from different lanes (where studied, where published, where reported, where patented) together.
5. Geography as a map: at least one country-level world map. Each map states what its values are (the lane: country an article is about; country of first-author affiliation; country of the publishing journal; patent assignee country), its window and unit, and how many items could be placed on a country. If a lane is empty, say so instead of drawing it.
6. Charts across dimensions: charts covering at least five of these seven dimensions: time; geography; comparison between countries or entities; composition (shares of stance, orientation or study tier); forecast; evidence magnitude (effect sizes or tiers of the key studies); and source mix (research literature vs health literature vs news vs patents). Each chart has a title, unit, window, source and a one-sentence reading, and backs a sentence in the text. No two charts show the same quantity.
7. Forecast: a three-year projection of at least one measured series, shown as the observed points plus a central path with lower and upper bounds. State the method, the baseline it was chosen against, the backtest error against a no-change baseline, the last observed period and the gap to today, and what the series measures and does not measure. A projection from memory must be labelled estimate; a projection of a real-world quantity (deaths, concentrations, cases) must carry its published source or the estimate label.
8. The whole evidence base, connected: the research literature, the clinical and health evidence (including the direction of risk-factor claims and the strongest effect sizes with their populations), the news record, and patents, each with traced numbers, plus at least two sentences that connect two of them into one argument (for example whether evidence and public attention move together, or whether India is where the problem is reported but not where it is studied). Where a source has nothing, say that it has nothing.
9. Policy options: a table with id="policy-options" and exactly these columns in this order: Option | Who acts | Evidence | Cost / benefit | Trade-off | Indicator. At least two options plus the status quo. "Who acts" names the level and the body (a ministry, a central board, state governments, municipal bodies, a regulator, Parliament), never "the government". "Evidence" cites the item behind the option with a source tag. "Cost / benefit" gives a figure with its source tag or the label (est.), or says "not measured". "Indicator" names a measurable series the Secretaries could track, defined in terms of the data in this briefing. Below the table: the recommended option and why it follows from the verdict and the forecast; the strongest evidence against the recommendation, with its source; and a short "what we do not know" list in which each gap is paired with the specific query that would close it.
10. Drill-down: under the headline numbers, the next layer (themes or subcategories, countries, the key documents) with identifiers (DOI, URL, label, country), and three to eight follow-up questions, each paired with the exact query that would answer it. If you have a tool, give the call and its arguments; if you do not, write the query in words.
11. Exports: at least three data tables as CSV (the time series; the country table; the key documents with identifiers and verbatim quotes), each with its source, window, unit, coverage flag and export date, each named in the text. Keep nulls as empty cells, never zeros.
12. Method and limits, placed beside the numbers they bound, not in a footer: the end date of the newest data and the gap to today; what each count is and is not (articles about a place, papers matching a phrase, patents by assignee); lanes; coverage; censored periods; the lag with which patents publish; thin evidence; and what would close each gap.
13. References: every document you rely on, with title, venue or publisher, year and a resolvable DOI or URL, each tied to the claim it supports, with quotes verbatim from the source.

RULES ON SOURCES
- Every number in the visible text carries an inline source tag: [c1], [c2] ... for a data query you ran during this task (declared in the calls list with its arguments); [r1], [r2] ... for an entry in References; or (est.) for a figure from memory. An untagged number is treated as unsourced.
- A chart, map, table, forecast or options-table figure whose values have no source and are not labelled estimate is scored as invented, and one invented element caps the whole briefing.
- An honest estimate label is never penalised for being an estimate. Say what the data cannot answer rather than filling the gap.
- Counted at most: 10 charts, 6 exports, 8 references tied to claims, 8 follow-up queries. Extras are ignored unless they are invented.

FORMAT
=== DELIVERABLE CONTRACT (identical for every respondent) ===
Return ONE self-contained HTML document inside a single ```html fenced block, and nothing outside it.
- Charts: Vega-Lite 5 loaded from cdn.jsdelivr.net exactly as
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega@5.30.0"></script>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-lite@5.21.0"></script>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-embed@6.26.0"></script>
  and rendered with vegaEmbed('#<chart id>', spec) into an element whose id equals the chart's manifest id,
  with the data inline in each spec ("data": {"values": [...]}); the only file a spec may load is the map file below.
- Maps: country-level choropleths using the GeoJSON served next to the report at the relative URL
  "world_india_official.geojson" (Vega-Lite data {"url": "world_india_official.geojson", "format": {"type": "json",
  "property": "features"}}; each feature has properties.iso3, properties.name and properties.id = ISO numeric;
  India is drawn with the official Survey of India outline). Join your values with a lookup transform on
  "properties.iso3". Do not use any other map file. In the manifest, map points are [country name or ISO alpha-3, value].
- Every number shown on the page carries a source tag: [c1] [c2] ... (a call you made, declared in the
  manifest), [r1] [r2] ... (an entry in References) or (est.) (an estimate from memory). A chart, map, table or
  forecast whose values have no source and are not labelled estimate is scored as invented.
- The page MUST contain <script type="application/json" id="report-manifest"> holding JSON with keys:
  "verdict": {"answer": "...", "decision": "...", "confidence": "high|medium|low - reason", "what_would_change": "..."},
  "charts": [ {"id", "kind": "line|bars|hbar|share|map|forecast", "title", "unit",
               "window": {"from": "YYYY-MM-DD", "to": "YYYY-MM-DD"}, "x": {"field": "period|year|label|country", "type": "temporal|ordinal|geo"},
               "series": [{"name", "source": "call:<feature>#<n> | ref:rN | estimate", "points": [[x, value], ...]}],
               "forecast": {"method": "...", "source": "call:<feature>#<n> | estimate", "horizon": "...",
                            "points": [[x, central, lower, upper], ...]}   (kind=forecast only),
               "caption", "supports": "the sentence on the page this chart backs, verbatim"} ],
  "exports": [ {"name": "file.csv", "source", "window": "from..to", "unit", "coverage": "full|partial|unknown", "csv": "header\nrow..."} ],
  "calls": [ {"id": "c1", "feature", "args", "used_for"} ... , {"id": "f1", "question", "feature", "args"} ... ],
  "references": [ {"id": "r1", "title", "venue", "year", "doi_or_url"} ]
  Every chart drawn on the page appears in the manifest with the same values; the visible page and the
  manifest must agree. "calls" may be [] if you ran no data queries. Follow-up entries (f1..) give a next
  question and the query that would answer it: a tool feature and args if you have a tool, else the query in words.


Answer from your own knowledge only; do not run commands or browse. You may include charts, maps, tables and projections from your knowledge, with each series' source given as a named published source (ref:rN) or as estimate. Do not run any commands or tools.

I do not want a literature summary; I want a decision briefing that tells me what the evidence says, where India stands against the world, where this is heading, what our options are, who would have to act, and what it would cost us to be wrong. My team will check every number against its source, so I would rather read "we cannot measure this" than a confident figure nobody can trace.

Build the briefing as one self-contained HTML page that I can open with nothing but the chart library loading from the network, and hand to the Secretaries. Lead with the decision.

WHAT THE BRIEFING MUST CONTAIN (each item is checked)
1. Verdict, first: the answer in one or two sentences; the decision it supports; confidence (high, medium or low) with the reason; what would change it. At most 150 words. Every number in it carries a source tag.
2. What the data shows: the measured picture, every number tagged, with what is measured separated from what is interpretation.
3. Trend over time: how attention and evidence on sugar-sweetened beverages, obesity and type 2 diabetes (central claim: sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes) have moved in the research literature (papers per year) and in the news (articles per month) over a stated window, with the change quantified (growth factor, peak with its date, direction) and the newest incomplete period marked rather than plotted as a collapse.
4. India against the world: at least one comparison on one scale and one window (India's share and lift in coverage; India's place in where the research is done and where it is published; comparators such as China, the United States, the United Kingdom and one neighbour of your choice), with the ratio or delta stated and the baseline defined. Never add numbers from different lanes (where studied, where published, where reported, where patented) together.
5. Geography as a map: at least one country-level world map. Each map states what its values are (the lane: country an article is about; country of first-author affiliation; country of the publishing journal; patent assignee country), its window and unit, and how many items could be placed on a country. If a lane is empty, say so instead of drawing it.
6. Charts across dimensions: charts covering at least five of these seven dimensions: time; geography; comparison between countries or entities; composition (shares of stance, orientation or study tier); forecast; evidence magnitude (effect sizes or tiers of the key studies); and source mix (research literature vs health literature vs news vs patents). Each chart has a title, unit, window, source and a one-sentence reading, and backs a sentence in the text. No two charts show the same quantity.
7. Forecast: a three-year projection of at least one measured series, shown as the observed points plus a central path with lower and upper bounds. State the method, the baseline it was chosen against, the backtest error against a no-change baseline, the last observed period and the gap to today, and what the series measures and does not measure. A projection from memory must be labelled estimate; a projection of a real-world quantity (deaths, concentrations, cases) must carry its published source or the estimate label.
8. The whole evidence base, connected: the research literature, the clinical and health evidence (including the direction of risk-factor claims and the strongest effect sizes with their populations), the news record, and patents, each with traced numbers, plus at least two sentences that connect two of them into one argument (for example whether evidence and public attention move together, or whether India is where the problem is reported but not where it is studied). Where a source has nothing, say that it has nothing.
9. Policy options: a table with id="policy-options" and exactly these columns in this order: Option | Who acts | Evidence | Cost / benefit | Trade-off | Indicator. At least two options plus the status quo. "Who acts" names the level and the body (a ministry, a central board, state governments, municipal bodies, a regulator, Parliament), never "the government". "Evidence" cites the item behind the option with a source tag. "Cost / benefit" gives a figure with its source tag or the label (est.), or says "not measured". "Indicator" names a measurable series the Secretaries could track, defined in terms of the data in this briefing. Below the table: the recommended option and why it follows from the verdict and the forecast; the strongest evidence against the recommendation, with its source; and a short "what we do not know" list in which each gap is paired with the specific query that would close it.
10. Drill-down: under the headline numbers, the next layer (themes or subcategories, countries, the key documents) with identifiers (DOI, URL, label, country), and three to eight follow-up questions, each paired with the exact query that would answer it. If you have a tool, give the call and its arguments; if you do not, write the query in words.
11. Exports: at least three data tables as CSV (the time series; the country table; the key documents with identifiers and verbatim quotes), each with its source, window, unit, coverage flag and export date, each named in the text. Keep nulls as empty cells, never zeros.
12. Method and limits, placed beside the numbers they bound, not in a footer: the end date of the newest data and the gap to today; what each count is and is not (articles about a place, papers matching a phrase, patents by assignee); lanes; coverage; censored periods; the lag with which patents publish; thin evidence; and what would close each gap.
13. References: every document you rely on, with title, venue or publisher, year and a resolvable DOI or URL, each tied to the claim it supports, with quotes verbatim from the source.

RULES ON SOURCES
- Every number in the visible text carries an inline source tag: [c1], [c2] ... for a data query you ran during this task (declared in the calls list with its arguments); [r1], [r2] ... for an entry in References; or (est.) for a figure from memory. An untagged number is treated as unsourced.
- A chart, map, table, forecast or options-table figure whose values have no source and are not labelled estimate is scored as invented, and one invented element caps the whole briefing.
- An honest estimate label is never penalised for being an estimate. Say what the data cannot answer rather than filling the gap.
- Counted at most: 10 charts, 6 exports, 8 references tied to claims, 8 follow-up queries. Extras are ignored unless they are invented.
